## The idea

Add another stacked third above a triad and a fourth melodic line enters the
chord. C-E-G-B sounds spacious, with B pressed close to the upper C. Lower that
note to B-flat and the chord acquires another direction. The lower major triad
has not moved; the seventh has changed the harmony's tension and likely
destination.

A *seventh chord* contains four tones built in thirds. Major seventh, minor
seventh, dominant seventh, and half-diminished seventh each correspond to a
different offset array. The dominant seventh is especially revealing. G-B-D-F
contains the tritone B-F, and both of those notes lie a semitone away from stable
tones in a C-major tonic chord.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 76
use_synth :piano

qualities = {
  major_7: [0, 4, 7, 11],
  minor_7: [0, 3, 7, 10],
  dominant_7: [0, 4, 7, 10],
  half_diminished_7: [0, 3, 6, 10]
}

qualities.each do |name, offsets|
  notes = offsets.map { |offset| note(:c4) + offset }
  puts name
  play_chord notes, release: 1.7
  sleep 2
  notes.each { |pitch| play pitch, release: 0.35; sleep 0.4 }
  sleep 1
end

dominant = [55, 59, 62, 65]
tonic = [55, 60, 64, 67]

define :play_resolution do |from, to, solo|
  voices = solo.nil? ? (0...from.length).to_a : [solo]
  voices.each do |index|
    in_thread do
      play from[index], release: 1.4, amp: 0.7
      sleep 2
      play to[index], release: 1.8, amp: 0.7
    end
  end
  sleep 4
end

play_resolution dominant, tonic, nil
4.times { |voice| play_resolution dominant, tonic, voice }
```

Each quality first sounds as a block, where four pitches merge into one harmony,
and then as an arpeggio, where its offset pattern becomes easier to follow. The
G7-to-C resolution is subsequently dismantled by voice. Listen for B rising to
C while F falls to E. Those contrary semitone motions supply much of the
cadence's force.

## Change one thing

1. Remove F from `dominant`. G major can still point toward C through B's
   leading-tone motion, but the tritone and its contracting pair of resolutions
   have disappeared.
2. Send F upward to G rather than downward to E. G belongs to the arriving tonic
   chord, so the harmony still closes, but the tritone expands instead of
   contracting. Compare that motion with the stronger contrary semitone pair.
3. Lower B to B-flat. The interval inside the chord changes, and B-flat no longer
   leads upward to C in the same way. Hear the loss of ordinary C-major dominant
   function before treating it as a one-integer edit.

## Why it works

Seventh-chord quality can be represented as offsets from a root. Major 7 and
dominant 7 differ only at the top note. Minor 7 lowers both third and seventh;
half-diminished 7 lowers the fifth as well. The names make these sound like four
separate objects, while the arrays reveal a close family connected by local
changes.

Inside G7, B and F span six semitones. Each is one semitone from a stable C-major
tone. When B rises and F falls, the tritone contracts into the major third C-E.
G can remain as a common tone, and D can move to either C or E. The ear groups
the result as a chord progression, but its explanatory motion belongs to four
simultaneous melodies.

The `solo` argument is a diagnostic switch. It lets one indexed melody sound
without rewriting the underlying chord data. Dense harmony often conceals the
short movement that creates its effect, so isolating voices is the harmonic
equivalent of inspecting one variable in a crowded trace.

Function depends on root and context as well as quality. C-E-G-B-flat is a C
dominant seventh and points readily toward F. C-E-G-B is a C major seventh and
can colour a tonic in C major. One offset makes that difference, which means the
shared lower triad cannot name the chord's likely job. Listen to the seventh
before reducing these qualities to neighbouring dictionary entries.

Doubling belongs to another layer. The offset arrays state each chord tone once,
but a four-voice arrangement may double the tonic and omit the fifth. That is a
voicing policy applied after construction. Keeping it separate allows one chord
record to feed a keyboard block, an arpeggio, or four independent lines without
changing the harmonic definition.

## Take it further

Extend Lesson 27's candidate set with inversions of G7 and C. Search for a pair
in which B moves to C, F moves to E, no line leaps more than five semitones, and
no voices cross. Print the chosen voicings and their total movement. Then play
the full resolution followed by each line alone, checking that the small motions
you encoded remain audible when the chord is reassembled.
